Traditionally, the Lantern hierarchy divides cosmic power strictly along the seven separate colors of the Emotional Spectrum, with each independent Corps governed by its own leadership and central power battery. Rival and allied factions are also locked into single emotional wavelengths, with Corps like the Blue Lanterns of hope and the Indigo Tribe of compassion usually on good terms with the Green Lanterns, while Sinestro's Yellow Lanterns of fear and Atrocitus's Red Lanterns of clash with the heroes.

items.title: 5 Classic Books Published After Their Authors' Deaths
items.summary: There’s a problem with genius : It makes everything seem so easy. When it comes to literary classics , there’s the assumption of inevitability. When a writer scribbles a masterpiece, the book is immediately published, and it grows in popularity until, a century later, it sits on a bookstore shelf with a little sticker declaring it essential reading. But that’s the stuff of fairy tales. Publishers turn down manuscripts. Finished novels spend decades in drawers. Governments suppress voices. Writers die.
items.t: 5 Classic Books Published After Their Authors' Deaths

items.title: Marvel Announces The Death Of Jessica Jones
items.summary: It's generally fair to assume that in the comics world, nobody truly stays dead, and in the case of Marvel , there's some extra fun to be had beyond simple retcons and resurrections. For the Marvel Zombies metaseries, the publisher thus gets the opportunities to kill off and/or turn iconic superheroes and villains into horrific undead adversaries, with its latest story being no exception. Trapped under a force field intended to contain a zombie outbreak orchestrated by Gorgon and the Hunger, Frank Castle suddenly encounters the horror of having to kill allies or even friends. In the case of one such ally, it's even meant having to kill a longtime partner like Jessica Jones.
items.t: Marvel Announces The Death Of Jessica Jones

items.title: ‘NCIS’ Co-Creator Officially Sells Series After 20+ Years
items.summary: When Donald P. Bellisario created the military legal drama procedural JAG over 30 years ago, he couldn't have had any idea what kind of juggernaut franchise he was spawning. The prolific Emmy nominee had a hand in creating his fair share of iconic television series, including the original Magnum P.I. starring Tom Selleck , and Quantum Leap , but the three-letter acronym has cast the longest shadow thanks to the much bigger giant that would come out of it — NCIS . While the parent series would go on to last for ten seasons on CBS , the decision to introduce Leroy Jethro Gibbs ( Mark Harmon ) and the Major Case Response Team cemented its place in television history. Now, after over 500 episodes and seven spin-offs across over 23 years, he's bowing out completely.
items.t: ‘NCIS’ Co-Creator Officially Sells Series After 20+ Years

items.title: 14th review – Ava DuVernay takes on a bully president and his viper’s-nest court of Maga sycophants
items.summary:
DuVernay’s follow-up to her dissection of the 13th Amendment to the US constitution is a vehement and exhilarating defence of democracy

Ava DuVernay’s previous documentary 13th, energised by the Black Lives Matter movement, was a brilliant polemic about the 13th Amendment to the US constitution, which she argued perpetuated a link between slavery and prison for African American men. Ten years later, and after an almost continuous decade of Trumpism, DuVernay has made a follow-up film about the 14th Amendment, and she has evidently arrived at a rather different attitude to the constitution and its authors’ intentions and good faith. Now she sees the enemy as Maga and the constitution as something that must be defended against a tinpot bully president and his viper’s-nest court of sycophants.

The shift in view is not acknowledged, but the overall effect is similar. Utilising a gallery of very smart talking-head interviewees, including conservative Republicans, DuVernay has mounted a vehement and exhilarating defence of what might be called the second American Enlightenment, created by the 13th, 14th and 15th “reconstruction” amendments, drawn up between 1865 and 1870 after the American civil war. The 14th…

items.title: ‘I said no thanks to the casting couch. But other actresses had problems’: Jane Alexander on 50 years of stardom
items.summary:
The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali

Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states.

Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role.

items.title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
items.summary:
The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest in a growing wave of movies steeped in nostalgia for a heyday in stark contrast to its current ruination

If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s

items.title: ‘I needed to purge it out of me’: the shocking true story behind harrowing drama Josephine
items.summary:
Writer-director Beth de Araújo witnessed a brutal sexual assault as a child and has turned her experience into one of the year’s most powerful movies

The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong.

So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’”

items.t: ‘I needed to purge it out of me’: the shocking true story behind harrowing drama Josephine

items.title: The Slightest Touch review – running marathons in Colin Farrell and Emma Fogarty’s odd-couple friendship
items.summary:
The pair, who met in 2010, are shown preparing for the Dublin race to raise awareness of Fogarty’s epidermolysis bullosa in Rachel Fleit’s considerate documentary

The personal scenes in this film from Rachel Fleit have been carefully controlled and curated, the privacy of both parties being important, for different and understandable reasons. But it is an unexpectedly intimate, emotional piece of work, a big-hearted odd-couple story, which is perhaps slightly more complex than at first appears.

Emma Fogarty is a smart, garrulous woman from Abbeyleix in County Laois in the Republic of Ireland who has EB: epidermolysis bullosa, a rare condition which means that her skin is permanently, agonisingly painful and requires a daily calvary of bandaging and re-bandaging. While getting an award at the People of the year event in 2010 for her campaigning work educating the public about this illness, Emma met and struck up a friendship with Colin Farrell, a supporter and patron of the EB charity Debra Ireland.

items.title: Post your questions for Danny Boyle
items.summary:
The Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire and 28 Days Later director is preparing to launch his biopic of Rupert Murdoch’s early years as a British tabloid mogul. In anticipation of its New Year release, the director will be taking your questions

You name it, Danny Boyle has probably directed a movie about it. He’s done zombies in 28 Days Later, astronauts hurtling towards the sun in Sunshine, a man trapped under a boulder in 127 Hours, a world without the Beatles in Yesterday and junkies in Trainspotting.

Boyle was born in Radcliffe near Manchester in 1956, and was heading towards the priesthood until, aged 14, a priest of all people talked him out of it. Instead he went into theatre, became deputy director of the Royal Court, then swerved into television, directing Inspector Morse among other things. His first film, Shallow Grave, arrived in 1994; two years later Trainspotting tore British cinema a new one. In 2009, Slumdog Millionaire won him the best director Oscar. He also masterminded the London 2012 Olympics opening ceremony, somehow squeezing industrial chimneys, NHS beds, James Bond, Mr Bean and the history of British pop into one stadium.

Continue reading...
items.t: Post your questions for Danny Boyle

items.title: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
items.summary:
For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception. Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real. Is that why his film has been so successful?

• This article does not contain major spoilers

Sometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there.

Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding.

Continue reading...
items.t: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
